title: Threat Actors and Vectors
objective: By the end of this lesson you can rank threat actors by capability and intent, name what motivates each, and map the attack vectors they prefer.

blocks.text: Security answers change depending on the opponent. A bored teenager with downloaded tools requires one defense; a funded state team that writes its own exploits requires another. The exam will describe an actor and ask you to infer intent, funding, or sophistication. Start with motivation.

An advanced persistent threat (APT) is the label for a well-resourced actor, usually state-linked, that gains access and stays quietly inside for a long time. The keywords that signal an APT on the exam are patience, long dwell time, and targeted espionage rather than quick profit.

items: Email: phishing remains the top opening move.
SMS and messaging: smishing and malicious links on phones.
Removable media: infected USB drives, sometimes dropped on purpose.
Web: compromised sites, malicious downloads, typosquatted domains.
Supply chain: attacking a trusted vendor or software update to reach the real target.
Unsupported systems: unpatched, end-of-life software with public exploits.
Insider access: legitimate credentials used for illegitimate aims.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Scenario keywords map to actors: quick defacement points to a script kiddie or hacktivist; a ransom note with a professional payment portal points to organized crime; months of quiet data theft points to an APT. Match the behavior, then the label.

Threat intelligence feeds, threat actors' known patterns, and intelligence fusion (combining several sources into one picture) all help defenders predict likely attackers. You will meet these again in the attack-frameworks lesson; here the takeaway is that knowing the actor tells you which vectors to watch first.

blocks.title: Actor profiling drill
steps: Read these three mini scenarios: (1) a payroll clerk exports data two weeks before resigning; (2) a hospital's files are locked with a ransom demand; (3) a defense contractor finds an eleven-month-old stealthy backdoor.
Name the vector each one used.
For each, name one control that would have stopped it earliest.
blocks.expected: 1: malicious insider via legitimate access; least privilege and access reviews. 2: organized crime via phishing; MFA and backups. 3: APT via supply chain or unpatched system; patching and network segmentation.

cheatsheet: Capability ladder: script kiddie < hacktivist < organized crime < nation-state/APT.
Motivations: money (crime), ideology (hacktivist), revenge (insider), espionage and disruption (APT).
Top vectors: email phishing, messaging, removable media, web, supply chain, unsupported systems, insider access.
APT tell: patient, long dwell time, targeted; label appears when profit is absent.

checkpoint.prompt: An energy utility discovers malware that hid quietly for months while slowly mapping its control network. No ransom was demanded. Which actor fits best?
checkpoint.explanation: Long dwell time, stealthy reconnaissance, critical-infrastructure targeting, and no profit motive all point to an APT. Quick disruption or publicity would fit other actors.
